source.title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
source.authors: Ryan Lee; Jacob Biloki; Edward J. Hu; Jonathan May

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendix tables and figures' descriptions, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out test loss over model sizes and compute budgets and fits scaling curves, using an isoFLOP approach on new transformer architectures.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling results for four architectures. The downstream benchmark scores are also recorded, but they compare architectures at one compute budget and do not test downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss. Early-exit and routing analyses do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study runs isoFLOP sweeps across four budgets (5e16 to 1e18 FLOPs) for four architectures and fits L ∝ N^−α through the compute-optimal points. It reports α = 0.076 (Base) and 0.077 (Looped-MoE), matching Kaplan's 0.076. This bears directly on V1 in the original isoFLOP and test-loss setting. The study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that dense looping scales worse than Base, while swapping dense FFNs for top-k MoE makes Looped-MoE scale better than Base, through a lower loss offset with near-identical exponent. They attribute this to routing divergence across loops. They also find that loop boundaries give better training-free early-exit trade-offs, and that Looped-MoE has the best downstream average among Base, Looped and Looped-MoE.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an isoFLOP sweep, test loss and power-law fitting similar to the scaling-law approach, but studies dense, sparse and looped architectures in a limited-scale controlled comparison rather than reproducing the original model suite.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture choice changes the reported scaling offset and performance ordering. The study uses quadratic fits to select compute-optimal points and fits power laws through those points. It holds depth constant while scaling width because µP transfer does not hold when depth changes.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched active parameters and compute, the architectures share roughly the same loss-scaling slope but differ in offset: MoE is best, then Looped-MoE, Base, and Looped.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-tying (looping) and sparse experts shift the loss scaling curve's offset without changing its exponent, when active parameters are used as N.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1e18 FLOPs, Core 9 downstream averages are Looped-MoE 39.6, Base 38.7, Looped 37.4 and MoE 36.4. MoE has the best test loss but the lowest downstream score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across architectures at a fixed compute budget, lower pretraining loss does not guarantee better downstream averages.

record.problems: The tested scale is limited: the authors report not scaling beyond 305M/711M active/stored parameters and plan future validation at 1B and 7B. Only four compute budgets are used. Numerical scaling exponents are stated for Base and Looped-MoE, but not for Looped or MoE. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Early-exit perplexity, routing-overlap and intermediate-output-convergence findings were omitted because they do not measure the claim versions. Individual OLMES task scores in Tables 4 and 6 were omitted in favor of the separately reported Core 9 aggregate for each architecture.

untested.parts: Covers only about 1.3 decades in parameters (16M–305M active) and compute (four budgets, 5e16–1e18). Loss versus tokens or compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecked is not fitted separately.
There is no check of small-run fits against larger runs. The authors assume extrapolation holds and defer validation to 1B/7B.
Compute-optimal points are selected, but no exponents for N_opt or D_opt versus C are reported.
Depth is held at 16 effective layers, and depth/width/aspect ratio are never varied at fixed parameter count.
Downstream scores are reported at a single budget, with no trend against scale or loss.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule and data are not varied, and there is no analysis of curve bending.

missing.what: No numerical compute-optimal loss values or per-budget optimal N are recorded or stated in the text. They would be needed to compare the offset gaps between architectures.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 labels are dropped: architecture-family comparisons (MoE, looping) are not V4's shape-at-fixed-N test. The record's V1 limits_scope label is dropped because the narrow range is an untested part, not a qualifying result. N counts active parameters including embeddings, which differs from Kaplan's non-embedding convention; the exponent match is nonetheless reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fitted loss-versus-parameter scaling at compute-optimal points over the reported model and compute ranges. It does not separately establish loss scaling with tokens or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks, or cover several orders of magnitude.
No reported test of predictions from fits on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger. The authors say they rely on this principle and aim to validate at 1B and 7B scales.
The study selects compute-optimal models at four budgets but does not report fitted growth exponents for optimal parameter and token counts against compute.
Compares dense, sparse, looped and non-looped architectures at matched active parameter counts and effective depth; it does not systematically vary depth and width independently over a wide range.
Only text pretraining is studied; no other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning or transfer.
Downstream benchmarks are reported for compute-optimal models at one compute budget, but no downstream performance trend with scale or pretraining loss is tested.
The study does not vary fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules or data to test fit dependence or curve bending.

rows.note: The study reports the fitted exponent and says the Base isoFLOP curves are shown. The architecture comparisons also report that Base performs better than dense Looped but worse than MoE and Looped-MoE.
